newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil seen shedding image as ADR weakling in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Brazil seen shedding image as ADR weakling in 1997.

text.p: Brazil is likely to shed its image as a weakling in the surging American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) market next year when up to a dozen Brazilian companies may list on U.S. stock markets, experts said.
"We're very optimistic about companies from Brazil coming and listing on U.S. markets," said Joe Velli, who heads the ADR department for The Bank of New York.

Velli, speaking at a seminar on ADRs, said 25 to 30 Latin American firms are expected to enter U.S. markets in the next 12 to 18 months and seven to 12 Brazilian firms are likely to list on U.S. stock markets via level 2 or level 3 ADRs.

Similarly, Raymond Schortemeier, head of international business development for the New York Stock Exchange, said he expects "maybe a half-dozen" Brazilian companies to seek listings on the New York bourse.
"Brazil definitely is the most under-represented country that we have on the New York Stock Exchange. We hope to change that in the near future," he said.

Currently, the shares of 25 Brazilian firms trade in the United States. But just two of those companies -- federal telecoms giant Telebras and private pulp and paper producer Aracruz Celulose S.A. -- hold top-shelf level 3 ADR listings, allowing them to trade and raise capital on U.S. stock markets.
By comparison, 23 Mexican, 18 Chilean, 10 Argentine and four Peruvian firms trade on the New York stock exchange, the world's busiest.

Level 1 ADRs may trade over-the-counter (OTC) in the U.S. but may not list on a U.S. stock market, while level 2 allows a listing and level 3 means a firm may list and raise fresh capital on a U.S. exchange.

ADR experts said the number of Brazilian firms trading on U.S. bourses will likely jump in 1997 due to privatizations, the growing need to raise money and the large number of local which already have level 1 status.
"Many companies that established level 1 ADR programs several years ago are upgrading," Velli said.

Also, "newly privatized companies will go straight to level 3 to raise money" while inceasing competition for capital will drive more firms to the New York bourse where they will enjoy greater visibility, he said.
Starting next year, Brazil plans to privatize some of its largest state companies including mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, state power firm Eletrobras and others.
Experts project a sharp rise in ADR issues in coming years as U.S. investors' appetite for non-U.S. securities continues to grow.

U.S. investors' holdings in non-U.S. securities are estimated to total $400 billion by year's end, or six percent of portfolios. Those figures are expected to grow to $2.1 trillion and 10 percent by 2000, according to Bank of New York.
The trend is likely to be reflected in ADR growth, with Latin America continuing to lead the world in new ADR issues, Velli said.
